kitaqgb/kitaqgb/CodeGenerator.cs:1799

__cgb_safe_set_hdma1

Write HDMA1 ($FF51), the high byte of the CGB DMA source address. This configures the source; it neither copies data nor starts a transfer. Set HDMA2 for the low byte.

Syntax

c
void __cgb_safe_set_hdma1(u8 value);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

value

Register value as u8 (0–255). The bit meanings for this particular register are given above; the function accepts a byte, not a pointer or a byte count.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Writes are guarded by the compiler's CGB-mode check and do nothing in DMG mode. Safe denotes this mode guard only. The call does not save or restore the previous register value.

One block is 16 bytes. New transfers support 1–128 blocks (16–2048 bytes), so control value 0 means 16 bytes, not an empty transfer. GDMA pauses the CPU until complete. HBlank DMA transfers one block per visible-line HBlank and runs across frames; the caller must poll or otherwise track completion before reusing its data.

Use GDMA with the LCD off or within a sufficiently long writable period. Start HBlank DMA with the LCD running, outside STAT mode 0; this sample starts it in VBlank. Do not change source banks, destination VBK or the source data while it is active. HALT pauses HBlank DMA too. No wait, interrupt protection or source/destination range check is added by these setters.

Read $FF55 separately: bit 7 clear means active; $FF means completed. After cancellation, bit 7 is set and bits 0–6 retain remaining blocks minus one. Cancellation does not undo copied bytes. Only issue a cancel command while a transfer is active; otherwise bit 7 clear starts GDMA. Keep the entire transfer inside valid source memory and the destination VRAM bank; do not rely on address overflow.

These HDMA register setters control CGB hardware DMA. __vram_copy_dma is a separate compiler alias for a CPU copy loop; its name does not make it use this DMA controller.

Usage example

c
__cgb_safe_set_hdma1(0xC6); // Source high byte: fixed-WRAM buffer at $C600.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The complete program compares three transfer paths using a 16-byte-aligned buffer at $C600. GDMA copies 32 bytes to $8010: at screen (16,24) a red 8 × 8 triangle grows from one leftmost pixel to a full bottom row, followed at (24,24) by a red one-pixel square outline. HBlank DMA copies 32 bytes to $8030: at (16,48) a blue 4 × 8 left half-tile is followed at (24,48) by a blue 8 × 8 square. These are actual transferred tile patterns, not numerical placeholders.

The CANCELED row contains a green 4 × 8 half-tile at (16,72) and a green 8 × 8 square at (24,72), initially written by the CPU. A two-block HBlank transfer targeting these tiles is armed and canceled in the same VBlank, before its first block; $FF55 must read $81, and both patterns must remain unchanged after a frame. On DMG, the first two rows stay blank and only these two sentinels appear in black. Text remains black on white. FAILED CHECKS 000 also checks copied bytes and completion status. The test covers dual-mode DMG/CGB and CGB-only execution in KOKURA; partial cancellation, double speed and real hardware are not tested.

Write one byte to the sprite (OBJ) palette data register OCPD/OBPD at $FF6B on CGB. __cgb_safe_set_ocpd is another name for the same register. The associated index register selects the byte position; a full RGB15 color requires a low byte and a high byte.

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Palette and guarded register writes do nothing in DMG mode. Here, safe means a CGB-mode guard, not a PPU access wait or a critical section. __cgb_safe_set_svbk

Write the raw WRAM selector SVBK ($FF70) on CGB. Hardware uses bits 0–2; raw values 0 and 1 both map bank 1 at $D000–$DFFF. For example, 8 also maps bank 1. Unlike __svbk_set, this guarded setter permits a dual-mode target and does not return the previous bank.

Syntax

c
void __cgb_safe_set_svbk(u8 value);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

value

Register value as u8 (0–255). The bit meanings for this particular register are given above; the function accepts a byte, not a pointer or a byte count.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Writes are guarded by the compiler's CGB-mode check and do nothing in DMG mode. Safe denotes this mode guard only. The call does not save or restore the previous register value.

Switching banks changes every access in $D000–$DFFF; fixed WRAM at $C000–$CFFF stays mapped. Keep the stack and all state needed during the switch outside the switched window. The sample uses --stack-bank=fixed and explicitly located fixed-WRAM state. Coordinate interrupts and banked DMA with the switch; these APIs add no critical section.

The values choose an 8 × 8 red square at (16,24) and a blue one-pixel 8 × 8 square outline at (16,48). Six separate invalid-build fixtures verify KQ2103 for DMG/dual targets and KQ2102 for constant banks 0 and 8. Increment software nesting depth and execute DI.

Syntax

if (funcName == "__critical_leave")
            {
                if (args.Length != 1) Error(expr, "__critical_leave(token) expects 1 argument");

                CompileIntoA(args[0]);
                EmitAsm("LD_B_A"); // token

                AsmOperand clAfterDec = MakeUniqueLabel("critleave_afterdec");
                AsmOperand clDone = MakeUniqueLabel("critleave_done");

                EmitLoadA(CriticalDepthVar);
                EmitAsm("OR_A");
                EmitAsm("JR_Z", clAfterDec);
                EmitAsm("DEC_A");
                EmitStoreA(CriticalDepthVar);
                EmitLabel(clAfterDec);

                // Re-enable only for outermost token (token==0).
                EmitAsm("LD_A_B");
                EmitAsm("OR_A");
                EmitAsm("JR_NZ", clDone);
                EmitAsm("EI");
                EmitLabel(clDone);
                return;
            }
__dot2_q8_8

Compute a unsigned two-term dot product.

Syntax

c
u16 __dot2_q8_8(u16 a0, u16 a1, u8 b0, u8 b1);

Parameters

a0

Unsigned word, 0..65535.

a1

Unsigned word, 0..65535.

b0

Unsigned coefficient, 0..255.

b1

Unsigned coefficient, 0..255.

Return value

Each term is floor(a*b/256). Sum the terms; returns the low 16 bits.

Conditions and limits

GB products are divided by 256; signed results truncate toward zero. Q1.7 variants double that truncated result and can differ by one from exact division by 128. Terms are rounded separately; final addition wraps at 16 bits.

Usage example

c
// Compare literal coefficients with values read from RAM.
result[36]=__dot2_q8_8(513,769,64,127);
v0=513;v1=769;v2=64;v3=127;
result[37]=__dot2_q8_8(v0,v1,v2,v3);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Compare literal inputs with values stored in RAM. Representative results appear as unsigned 16-bit values; negatives use two’s-complement bit patterns. GB rescales fixed-point products, while FC returns integer products, so identical inputs need not give identical results.

The excerpt stores these 16-bit values: result[36]=509, result[37]=509. Each literal-input calculation matches its RAM-input counterpart. The screen shows representative values; the result array holds every result.

csharp
if (funcName == "__dot2_q8_8")
{
    if (args.Length != 4) Error(expr, "__dot2_q8_8 requires 4 arguments");
    LastCallReturnsHL = true;

    // Fast paths when coefficients are compile-time constants.
    // Special-case: 0 / power-of-two coefficients (u8) => shift instead of mul.
    if (TryGetU8Const(args[2], out int ax0) && (ax0 == 0) && TryGetU8Const(args[3], out int ay0) && (ay0 == 0))
    {
        CompileDiscard(args[0]);
        CompileDiscard(args[1]);
        EmitAsm("XOR_A");
        EmitAsm("LD_H_A");
        EmitAsm("LD_L_A");
        return;
    }
    if (TryGetU8Const(args[2], out int axOnly) && (axOnly == 0))
    {
        CompileDiscard(args[0]);
        // only y*ay
        if (!TryEmitDot2Pow2Term(args[1], args[3], signed: false, q1_7: false, out _))
        {
            CompileIntoHL(args[1]);
            EmitAsm("PUSH_HL");
            CompileIntoA(args[3]);
            EmitAsm("LD_C_A");
            EmitAsm("POP_HL");
            EmitMul16x8Shr8_HL("__dot2_y");
        }
        return;
    }
    if (TryGetU8Const(args[3], out int ayOnly) && (ayOnly == 0))
    {
        // only x*ax
        if (!TryEmitDot2Pow2Term(args[0], args[2], signed: false, q1_7: false, out _))
        {
            CompileIntoHL(args[0]);
            EmitAsm("PUSH_HL");
            CompileIntoA(args[2]);
            EmitAsm("LD_C_A");
            EmitAsm("POP_HL");
            EmitMul16x8Shr8_HL("__dot2_x");
        }
        // Preserve the scaled result while evaluating the zero-product input.
        EmitAsm("PUSH_HL");
        CompileDiscard(args[1]);
        EmitAsm("POP_HL");
        return;
    }

    // x*ax
    if (!TryEmitDot2Pow2Term(args[0], args[2], signed: false, q1_7: false, out _))
    {
        CompileIntoHL(args[0]);
        EmitAsm("PUSH_HL");
        CompileIntoA(args[2]);
        EmitAsm("LD_C_A");
        EmitAsm("POP_HL");
        EmitMul16x8Shr8_HL("__dot2_x");
    }
    EmitAsm("PUSH_HL");

    // y*ay
    if (!TryEmitDot2Pow2Term(args[1], args[3], signed: false, q1_7: false, out _))
    {
        CompileIntoHL(args[1]);
        EmitAsm("PUSH_HL");
        CompileIntoA(args[3]);
        EmitAsm("LD_C_A");
        EmitAsm("POP_HL");
        EmitMul16x8Shr8_HL("__dot2_y");
    }
    EmitAsm("POP_DE");
    EmitAsm("ADD_HL_DE");
    return;
}

__farcall

Call a named, zero-argument function using the supplied bank number. When a bank change is needed, a helper in fixed ROM restores the caller's bank after the function returns.

Syntax

c
__farcall(bank, function_name);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

bank

An unsigned 8-bit ROM-bank number. For a call, it must agree with the function's placement; for a read, it selects the source mapping. Use the target cartridge's valid range.

func

The declared name of a function with no parameters. A variable holding a function address is not accepted by this named-call intrinsic. The bank argument is not forwarded as a callback parameter.

Return value

The called function's result type determines the result. A void callback yields no value; u8 and u16 callbacks return their scalar value. The displayed sample uses void callbacks.

Conditions and limits

These calls do not forward user arguments or make the callback interrupt-reentrant. Keep the callback's own data, stack and interrupt use valid. The bank-restoring call paths are tested with nested calls and repeated calls; physical hardware and arbitrary interrupt interleavings are not covered by this example.

These GB bank interfaces carry eight bank bits and do not set the ninth MBC5 bank bit. Cartridge rules still apply, including mapper-specific treatment of bank zero. The example explicitly uses MBC5 banks 1–3; do not mix this state with untracked raw mapper writes.

Usage example

c
__farcall(3,callback);
bank_expect(callback_count==2 && callback_byte==0xD3,16);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

At this point in the complete program, __farcall raises callback_count to 2. The callback reads D3 from bank 3. A later near read of B2 from home2 verifies that execution returned with bank 2 mapped.

The complete program teaches how a bank number and near address identify data, how callbacks cross banks, and how to distinguish the library's record from the actual mapping. All displayed numbers are hexadecimal. BANK IN and BANK OUT must show 02, BYTE HEX D3, WORD HEX 5C7A, and both FAILED CHECKS and FIRST FAILURE 00. CGB and FC display blue text; DMG displays black text.

CALL COUNT is 03: far_call, __farcall and __farcall_ptr each invoke the callback once.

Implementation and source

kitaqgb/kitaqgb/CodeGenerator.cs:7202

kitaqgb/kitaqgb/CodeGenerator.cs:7262

csharp
if (funcName == "__farcall")
            {
                if (args.Length != 2) Program.Error("__farcall(bank, func) expects 2 arguments");
                if (!args[1].Match(Tag.Name, out string targetName)) Program.Error("__farcall(bank, func) requires 2nd argument to be a function name");

                // A named far call supplies no arguments. Reject data symbols
                // and callbacks that would otherwise read stale argument storage.
                CFunctionInfo targetInfo;
                if (!Functions.TryGetValue(targetName, out targetInfo))
                {
                    Error(expr, "__farcall requires a declared function name");
                    return;
                }
                if ((targetInfo.Parameters ?? Array.Empty<FieldInfo>()).Length != 0)
                {
                    Error(expr, "__farcall requires a callback with no parameters");
                    return;
                }
                Expr bankExpr = FoldConstants(args[0]);
                int targetBank = -1;
                if (targetInfo != null)
                {
                    targetBank = targetInfo.RomBank;
                    PrepareStructReturnDestination(expr, targetInfo.ReturnType, targetInfo, targetName);
                    if (targetInfo.ReturnType != null)
                        LastCallReturnsHL = ReturnsInHL(expr, targetInfo.ReturnType);
                }

                // A known bank permits direct dispatch when safe, otherwise request a fixed-bank thunk.
                if (TryResolveBankExprToConstU8(args[0], out int bankLiteral))
                {
                    int optimizedBank = bankLiteral & 0xFF;
                    bool farcallDirectOK = IsDirectCallBankSafe(optimizedBank, CurrentFunctionBank);
                    if (!farcallDirectOK)
                    {
                        string farcallThunkName = EnsureBank0Thunk(
                            targetName,
                            optimizedBank,
                            isStackCall: targetInfo != null && targetInfo.IsStackCall,
                            stackArgBytes: 0);
                        EmitAsm("CALL", new AsmOperand(farcallThunkName, AddressMode.Absolute));
                        RecordCallEdge(expr, targetName, optimizedBank, "farcall_bank_thunk", viaThunk: true, viaFarcall: true, actualArgSizes: new int[0], expectedArgSizes: new int[0]);
                    }
                    else
                    {
                        if (Program.CheckBankCalls && !InUnsafe && optimizedBank != 0)
                        {
                            AsmOperand ok = MakeUniqueLabel("kq_bank_ok");
                            EmitLoadA(RomBankVar);
                            EmitAsm("CP_IMM", new AsmOperand(optimizedBank & 0xFF, AddressMode.Immediate));
                            EmitAsm("JP_Z", ok);
                            EmitAsm("JP", EnsureCheckTrap());
                            EmitLabel(ok);
                        }

                        EmitAsm("CALL", new AsmOperand(targetName, AddressMode.Absolute));
                        RecordCallEdge(expr, targetName, optimizedBank, "farcall_direct", viaThunk: false, viaFarcall: true, actualArgSizes: new int[0], expectedArgSizes: new int[0]);
                    }
                    return;
                }

                // A = requested bank argument (runtime value)
                CompileIntoA(bankExpr);

                // Always dispatch via bank0 helper thunk.
                string thunkName = EnsureBank0RuntimeFarcallThunk(targetName);
                EmitAsm("CALL", new AsmOperand(thunkName, AddressMode.Absolute));
                RecordCallEdge(expr, targetName, targetBank, "farcall_intrinsic", viaThunk: true, viaFarcall: true, actualArgSizes: new int[0], expectedArgSizes: new int[0]);
                return;
            }

if (funcName == "__getwinmapbase")
{
    if (args.Length != 0) Error(expr, "__getwinmapbase requires 0 arguments");

    AsmOperand win_base0 = MakeUniqueLabel("getwinbase_base0");
    AsmOperand win_done  = MakeUniqueLabel("getwinbase_done");

    EmitAsm("LDH_A_MEM", new AsmOperand(0x40, AddressMode.HighMem)); // LCDC
    EmitAsm("AND_IMM", new AsmOperand(0x40, AddressMode.Immediate)); // bit6 (Window tile map display select)
    EmitAsm("JR_Z", win_base0);
    EmitAsm("LD_HL_IMM", new AsmOperand(0x9C00, AddressMode.Immediate16));
    EmitAsm("JR", win_done);
    EmitLabel(win_base0);
    EmitAsm("LD_HL_IMM", new AsmOperand(0x9800, AddressMode.Immediate16));
    EmitLabel(win_done);
    LastCallReturnsHL = true;
    return;
}

__padrep

Schedule one repeating action selected by mask. Among newly pressed eligible bits, choose the lowest set bit and emit it immediately. Otherwise keep the active action while it remains eligible and held. If that action ends, adopt the lowest remaining held bit without an immediate pulse. No eligible held bits clears the runtime state.

Syntax

c
u8 __padrep(u8* state, u8 keys, u8 trigger, u8 mask);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

state

Pointer to five writable, consecutive RAM bytes, for example u8 state[5]. The layout is [0] active button bit, [1] initial delay, [2] repeat interval, [3] elapsed initial-delay count, [4] elapsed repeat count. Allocate a separate state for each independent scheduler. Initialize it before use; a null pointer, fewer than five bytes, or sharing the same state between directional and general schedulers is not supported.

keys

Current full held-button mask in the GB BTN_* layout. Supply a snapshot from __readpad, the low byte of __readpadex, or input_current; the scheduler does not poll hardware itself.

trigger

Newly pressed bits for this update in the same layout as keys, normally keys & ~previous_keys or the high byte of __readpadex. Only include bits also present in keys. Passing the held mask every time falsely restarts the initial press on every call.

mask

Eligible GB button bits combined with |. Zero disables all actions and clears the runtime state. Multiple bits enable several candidates, but the function emits only one selected bit per call, not a combined pulse mask.

Return value

Zero when no action pulse is due; otherwise one of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. The nonzero result is a button bit, not a normalized Boolean or a count of repeats.

Conditions and limits

Shared masks: BTN_RIGHT=0x01, BTN_LEFT=0x02, BTN_UP=0x04, BTN_DOWN=0x08, BTN_A=0x10, BTN_B=0x20, BTN_SELECT=0x40, BTN_START=0x80. A set bit means held. This layout applies to input_* on both GB and FC; raw FC pad functions use a different order.

Initial delay, 0–255 scheduler calls. With a positive value N, the first held repeat occurs exactly N calls after the initial press pulse. With 0, the initial-delay equality case is skipped and the repeat interval determines when the first held pulse occurs. These counts are not milliseconds.

Interval for subsequent repeats, 0–255 calls. Positive N emits every N eligible held updates after the first repeat. Zero emits on every eligible held update after the initial delay, so 0 and 1 both give one pulse per update at that stage. With both delay and interval set to 0, each held update emits a pulse.

Call the scheduler once per intended input tick. It modifies the state on every call and does not wait for VBlank. If a held button is adopted without a new-press bit, that adoption call returns 0 and starts a fresh delay. These functions schedule one active action per state; input_repeat instead maintains independent timers for all eight buttons.

Usage example

c
result=__padrep(actions,keys,trigger,48); // A|B: select A, the lower bit.
    if (result!=0) action_pulses++;

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program feeds controlled button snapshots into four independent states to show exactly when a repeat fires. With delay 3 and interval 2, eight calls numbered 0–7 emit pulses on calls 0, 3, 5 and 7. RIGHT PULSES, DOWN PULSES, ACTION PULSES and ALIAS PULSES therefore each display 004. The general schedulers receive A and B together and select A (16). The program also checks initialization, reset, two-direction priority, release, adoption of an already held direction, zero timing values and an expression argument. CHECKS displays 057 and FAILED CHECKS must display 000. This is a deterministic state-processing example; it does not wait for you to press buttons.

__padrep_init

Initialize a caller-owned five-byte repeat state: clear the active action and both counters, and store the supplied initial delay and repeat interval. No buttons are read and no repeat pulse is emitted.

Syntax

c
void __padrep_init(u8* state, u8 das, u8 arr);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

state

Pointer to five writable, consecutive RAM bytes, for example u8 state[5]. The layout is [0] active button bit, [1] initial delay, [2] repeat interval, [3] elapsed initial-delay count, [4] elapsed repeat count. Allocate a separate state for each independent scheduler. Initialize it before use; a null pointer, fewer than five bytes, or sharing the same state between directional and general schedulers is not supported.

das

Initial delay, 0–255 scheduler calls. With a positive value N, the first held repeat occurs exactly N calls after the initial press pulse. With 0, the initial-delay equality case is skipped and the repeat interval determines when the first held pulse occurs. These counts are not milliseconds.

arr

Interval for subsequent repeats, 0–255 calls. Positive N emits every N eligible held updates after the first repeat. Zero emits on every eligible held update after the initial delay, so 0 and 1 both give one pulse per update at that stage. With both delay and interval set to 0, each held update emits a pulse.

Return value

None (void).

Usage example

c
__padrep_init(lr,3,2);
// Active action and counters are zero; delay and interval are retained.
expect(lr[0],0); expect(lr[1],3); expect(lr[2],2);
expect(lr[3],0); expect(lr[4],0);

// 2.21 __padrep_reset(state_ptr) -> void
// Resets runtime counters for PadRepeatState while keeping das/arr params:
// dirMask=0, dasCnt=0, arrCnt=0
// Treated as a compiler intrinsic (no C definition required).
if (funcName == "__padrep_reset")
{
    if (args.Length != 1) Error(expr, "__padrep_reset requires 1 argument (state*)");

    CompileIntoHL(args[0]);

    EmitAsm("XOR_A");
    EmitAsm("LD_HL_A"); // [0]=0 (dirMask)

    // [3]=0, [4]=0
    EmitAsm("PUSH_HL");
    EmitAsm("INC_HL"); EmitAsm("INC_HL"); EmitAsm("INC_HL"); // -> [3]
    EmitAsm("LD_HL_A");
    EmitAsm("INC_HL"); // -> [4]
    EmitAsm("LD_HL_A");
    EmitAsm("POP_HL");
    return;
}

__padrep_lr

Advance a single Left/Right repeat action. A new Right press emits 1 immediately; otherwise a new Left press emits 2. If both are newly pressed, Right wins. Without a new press, holding both directions returns 0 and freezes the counters; holding neither clears the runtime state.

__padrep_reset

Cancel the active action and clear both elapsed counters while preserving the configured delay and interval. Use this when closing a menu or changing input focus so a previous hold does not carry its repeat timing into the next interaction.

Syntax

c
void __padrep_reset(u8* state);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

state

Pointer to five writable, consecutive RAM bytes, for example u8 state[5]. The layout is [0] active button bit, [1] initial delay, [2] repeat interval, [3] elapsed initial-delay count, [4] elapsed repeat count. Allocate a separate state for each independent scheduler. Initialize it before use; a null pointer, fewer than five bytes, or sharing the same state between directional and general schedulers is not supported.

Return value

None (void).

Usage example

c
__padrep_reset(lr);
expect(lr[0],0); expect(lr[1],3); expect(lr[2],2);
expect(lr[3],0); expect(lr[4],0);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

This program feeds controlled button snapshots into four independent states to show exactly when a repeat fires. With delay 3 and interval 2, eight calls numbered 0–7 emit pulses on calls 0, 3, 5 and 7. RIGHT PULSES, DOWN PULSES, ACTION PULSES and ALIAS PULSES therefore each display 004. The general schedulers receive A and B together and select A (16). The program also checks initialization, reset, two-direction priority, release, adoption of an already held direction, zero timing values and an expression argument. CHECKS displays 057 and FAILED CHECKS must display 000. This is a deterministic state-processing example; it does not wait for you to press buttons.

__readpad

Read directions and action buttons from JOYP and combine them into the shared 8-bit button mask. Selects each JOYP group, performs two reads for settling, then restores the group-selection bits to 0x30.

Syntax

c
u8 __readpad();

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Return value

An 8-bit mask in the shared BTN_* layout. Several buttons may be set simultaneously; 0 means none.

Conditions and limits

Shared masks: BTN_RIGHT=0x01, BTN_LEFT=0x02, BTN_UP=0x04, BTN_DOWN=0x08, BTN_A=0x10, BTN_B=0x20, BTN_SELECT=0x40, BTN_START=0x80. A set bit means held. This layout applies to input_* on both GB and FC; raw FC pad functions use a different order.

This call reads a fresh hardware snapshot; it does not update input_* or nes_pad1_* cached state and does not generate pressed/released edges or repeats. Read once, save the result, and derive edges against your saved previous mask when needed.

Usage example

c
all_keys=__readpad(); // A + Right: 0x11, decimal 17.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Use this program to compare the three button-mask layouts and the packed press result. Hold A and Right together. ALL KEYS is 17; DIRECTIONS and BUTTONS LOW are each 1. With a previous mask of 0, EX CURRENT and EX NEW PRESS are both 17. Passing the current mask to the next read makes HELD PRESS 0. FAILED CHECKS must be 0. The values remain on screen after the snapshot, so releasing the buttons does not erase them.

    EmitAsm("LDH_MEM_A", p1);
    EmitAsm("LD_A_C");
    return;
}

__sdot2_q1_7

Compute a signed two-term dot product.

Syntax

c
u16 __sdot2_q1_7(u16 a0, u16 a1, u8 b0, u8 b1);

Parameters

a0

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

a1

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

b0

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

b1

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

Return value

Each term is 2*trunc(a*b/256). Sum the terms; returns the low 16 bits.

Conditions and limits

GB products are divided by 256; signed results truncate toward zero. Q1.7 variants double that truncated result and can differ by one from exact division by 128. Terms are rounded separately; final addition wraps at 16 bits.

Usage example

c
// Compare literal coefficients with values read from RAM.
result[20]=__sdot2_q1_7(-513,769,-64,127);
v0=-513;v1=769;v2=-64;v3=127;
result[21]=__sdot2_q1_7(v0,v1,v2,v3);
// Reverse coefficient signs and verify negative products.
result[22]=__sdot2_q1_7(-513,769,64,-127);
v0=-513;v1=769;v2=64;v3=-127;
result[23]=__sdot2_q1_7(v0,v1,v2,v3);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Compare literal inputs with values stored in RAM. Representative results appear as unsigned 16-bit values; negatives use two’s-complement bit patterns. GB rescales fixed-point products, while FC returns integer products, so identical inputs need not give identical results.

The excerpt stores these 16-bit values: result[20]=1018, result[21]=1018, result[22]=64518, result[23]=64518. Each literal-input calculation matches its RAM-input counterpart. The screen shows representative values; the result array holds every result.

        EmitAsm("ADD_HL_HL");

if (funcName == "__sdot2_q8_8")
{
    if (args.Length != 4) Error(expr, "__sdot2_q8_8 requires 4 arguments");
    LastCallReturnsHL = true;

    // Fast paths when coefficients are compile-time constants.
    // Special-case: 0 / power-of-two coefficients (s8 two's complement) => arithmetic shift instead of mul.
    if (TryGetS8Const(args[2], out int sax0) && (sax0 == 0) && TryGetS8Const(args[3], out int say0) && (say0 == 0))
    {
        CompileDiscard(args[0]);
        CompileDiscard(args[1]);
        EmitAsm("XOR_A");
        EmitAsm("LD_H_A");
        EmitAsm("LD_L_A");
        return;
    }
    if (TryGetS8Const(args[2], out int saxOnly) && (saxOnly == 0))
    {
        CompileDiscard(args[0]);
        // only y*ay
        if (!TryEmitDot2Pow2Term(args[1], args[3], signed: true, q1_7: false, out _))

__sdot3_q1_7

Compute a signed three-term dot product.

Syntax

c
u16 __sdot3_q1_7(u16 a0, u16 a1, u16 a2, u8 b0, u8 b1, u8 b2);

Parameters

a0

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

a1

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

a2

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

b0

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

b1

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

b2

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

Return value

Each term is 2*trunc(a*b/256). Sum the terms; returns the low 16 bits.

Conditions and limits

GB products are divided by 256; signed results truncate toward zero. Q1.7 variants double that truncated result and can differ by one from exact division by 128. Terms are rounded separately; final addition wraps at 16 bits.

Usage example

c
// Compare literal coefficients with values read from RAM.
result[16]=__sdot3_q1_7(-513,769,-1025,-64,127,-3);
v0=-513;v1=769;v2=-1025;v3=-64;v4=127;v5=-3;
result[17]=__sdot3_q1_7(v0,v1,v2,v3,v4,v5);
// Reverse coefficient signs and verify negative products.
result[18]=__sdot3_q1_7(-513,769,-1025,64,-127,3);
v0=-513;v1=769;v2=-1025;v3=64;v4=-127;v5=3;
result[19]=__sdot3_q1_7(v0,v1,v2,v3,v4,v5);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Compare literal inputs with values stored in RAM. Representative results appear as unsigned 16-bit values; negatives use two’s-complement bit patterns. GB rescales fixed-point products, while FC returns integer products, so identical inputs need not give identical results.

The excerpt stores these 16-bit values: result[16]=1042, result[17]=1042, result[18]=64494, result[19]=64494. Each literal-input calculation matches its RAM-input counterpart. The screen shows representative values; the result array holds every result.

__settile_fast

Write one tile-number byte to the tile map; this selects an existing tile image, not new pixel data.

The destination is always 0x9800 + 32*y + x, regardless of which maps LCDC selects for the background and window.

Does not wait for VRAM access. Call only while the LCD is off or within a caller-managed writable interval with enough time for the whole transfer.

Syntax

c
__settile_fast(x, y, tile);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

x, y

Coordinates in 8×8 tiles, each from 0 to 31. Keep the complete write inside the 32×32 map; coordinates are not clipped.

tile

Tile number, 0–255. LCDC bit 4 determines how the number addresses tile-image data. It is not a VRAM byte address.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Tile bytes go to the currently selected VRAM bank. On CGB, select bank 0 for tile numbers; this call does not switch banks for you.

The example uses gb_common.h: m_init() loads the supplied ASCII font with character codes as tile numbers. m_wait(); M_LCDC=0; stops the LCD during VBlank before unsafe transfers. The final LCDC value selects which map is visible.

Usage example

c
// __settile_fast
// Write one tile-number byte to the tile map; this selects an existing tile image, not
// new pixel data. The destination is always `0x9800 + 32*y + x`, regardless of which
// maps LCDC selects for the background and window.
// Expected: FAILED CHECKS 000, with the written tile data in the selected map.
#include "gb_tile_color_example.h"
void __settile_fast(u8 x, u8 y, u8 tile);

void main() {
    u8 failures;
    failures = 0;
    tile_color_example_begin();
    __settile_fast(2, 3, 'A');
    if (tile_example_read(0x9862, 0) != 'A') { failures++; }
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C62, 0) != 0) { failures++; }
    tile_example_finish(failures, 0);
}

Expected result

The selected map shows the written characters or filled area. The program reads back the addressed tile bytes and, on CGB, the attribute bytes; FAILED CHECKS 000 means those comparisons passed. Both maps initially contain zero, and the example selects 0x9C00 for BG/window before the demonstrated call, so a fixed-map call can be distinguished from a selected-map call. These examples perform the writes with the LCD off; they do not measure LCD-on timing.

On CGB, the sample characters and status text are blue on white. The setup gives palette 0 a blue ink color; it does not change the tile-map attributes. On DMG, the same characters are black on white.

Expected image: the following tile pattern starts at tile coordinates (x=2, y=3), or pixel coordinates (16,24). Each character occupies one 8×8 tile. Read the pattern from top to bottom and left to right; the surrounding tiles remain blank.

text
A

__settilebg16_buf

Write a 16×16-pixel cell into a RAM tile-map buffer: the four 8×8 tile numbers are tile,tile+1 on top and tile+2,tile+3 below. Values wrap at 256. This does not transfer anything to VRAM.

Syntax

c
__settilebg16_buf(buf, x, y, tile);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

buf

A RAM buffer with 32 bytes per tile row. A full 32×32 map needs 1024 bytes. The upper-left byte is at 64*y + 2*x; the four offsets are 0,1,32,33 from there.

x, y

Coordinates in 16×16-pixel cells, each from 0 to 15 for a full 32×32-tile buffer. These differ from the 8×8-tile coordinates used by scalar setters.

tile

Tile number, 0–255. LCDC bit 4 determines how the number addresses tile-image data. It is not a VRAM byte address.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

The example uses gb_common.h: m_init() loads the supplied ASCII font with character codes as tile numbers. m_wait(); M_LCDC=0; stops the LCD during VBlank before unsafe transfers. The final LCDC value selects which map is visible.

Usage example

c
// __settilebg16_buf
// Write a 16×16-pixel cell into a RAM tile-map buffer: the four 8×8 tile numbers are
// `tile,tile+1` on top and `tile+2,tile+3` below. Values wrap at 256. This does not
// transfer anything to VRAM.
// Expected: FAILED CHECKS 000, with the written tile data in the selected map.
#include "gb_tile_color_example.h"
u8 example_tiles[1024];
u8 example_attrs[1024];
void __memset(void* dest, u8 value, u16 len);
void __settilebg16_buf(u8* buf, u8 x, u8 y, u8 tile);
void __settilebg16cgb_buf(u8* tilebuf, u8* attrbuf, u8 x, u8 y, u8 tile, u8 attr);
void __settilebg16_flush(const u8* buf, u8 y, u8 x, u8 count);
void __settilebg16cgb_flush(const u8* tilebuf, const u8* attrbuf, u8 y, u8 x, u8 count);

void main() {
    u8 failures;
    failures = 0;
    tile_color_example_begin();
    __memset(example_tiles, 0, 1024);
    __memset(example_attrs, 0, 1024);
    __settilebg16_buf(example_tiles, 1, 1, 'A');
    // The buffer operation must not write to VRAM yet.
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C42, 0) != 0) { failures++; }
    // Transfer the prepared cell so its four characters can be seen.
    __settilebg16_flush(example_tiles, 1, 2, 2);
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C42, 0) != 'A') { failures++; }
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C43, 0) != 'B') { failures++; }
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C62, 0) != 'C') { failures++; }
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C63, 0) != 'D') { failures++; }
    if (example_tiles[66] != 'A') { failures++; }
    if (example_tiles[99] != 'D') { failures++; }
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C44, 0) != 0) { failures++; }
    tile_example_finish(failures, 1);
}

These examples perform the writes with the LCD off; they do not measure LCD-on timing.

__settilebg16_flush

Transfer two adjacent tile rows from the RAM buffer to the LCDC-selected BG map. The source offset is 64*y + x; count bytes are copied from that row and from the row 32 bytes below it.

Waits for writable VRAM when necessary. The LCD-on path uses interrupt masking and can enable interrupts afterward; it is not a promise to preserve the caller's interrupt state or to finish within one VBlank.

Syntax

c
__settilebg16_flush(buf, y, x, count);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

buf

Readable tile-map buffer with a 32-byte row stride. A full map occupies 1024 bytes. The two-buffer form takes separate tile-number and attribute arrays with the same layout; it does not interleave them.

y, x, count

Argument order is y,x,count. y is a 16-pixel cell row (0–15); x and count are 8-pixel tile units. Keep x+count <= 32. For one cell at (2,3), use y=3,x=4,count=2.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Tile bytes go to the currently selected VRAM bank. On CGB, select bank 0 for tile numbers; this call does not switch banks for you.

The example uses gb_common.h: m_init() loads the supplied ASCII font with character codes as tile numbers. m_wait(); M_LCDC=0; stops the LCD during VBlank before unsafe transfers. The final LCDC value selects which map is visible.

__settilebg16cgb_buf

Write a 16×16-pixel cell into a RAM tile-map buffer: the four 8×8 tile numbers are tile,tile+1 on top and tile+2,tile+3 below. Values wrap at 256. This does not transfer anything to VRAM.

Also write the same attr byte to all four corresponding cells in the separate attribute buffer. Both buffers are ordinary RAM, so this preparation also runs on DMG.

Syntax

c
__settilebg16cgb_buf(tilebuf, attrbuf, x, y, tile, attr);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

tilebuf, attrbuf

A RAM buffer with 32 bytes per tile row. A full 32×32 map needs 1024 bytes. The upper-left byte is at 64*y + 2*x; the four offsets are 0,1,32,33 from there.

x, y

Coordinates in 16×16-pixel cells, each from 0 to 15 for a full 32×32-tile buffer. These differ from the 8×8-tile coordinates used by scalar setters.

tile

Tile number, 0–255. LCDC bit 4 determines how the number addresses tile-image data. It is not a VRAM byte address.

attr

CGB attribute byte: bits 0–2 select palette 0–7; bit 3 selects tile-data bank; bits 5 and 6 flip horizontally and vertically; bit 7 sets BG/window priority. Keep unused bit 4 zero.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

The example uses gb_common.h: m_init() loads the supplied ASCII font with character codes as tile numbers. m_wait(); M_LCDC=0; stops the LCD during VBlank before unsafe transfers. The final LCDC value selects which map is visible.

Usage example

c
// __settilebg16cgb_buf
// Write a 16×16-pixel cell into a RAM tile-map buffer: the four 8×8 tile numbers are
// `tile,tile+1` on top and `tile+2,tile+3` below. Values wrap at 256. This does not
// transfer anything to VRAM. Also write the same `attr` byte to all four corresponding
// cells in the separate attribute buffer. Both buffers are ordinary RAM, so this
// preparation also runs on DMG.
// Expected: FAILED CHECKS 000, with the written tile data in the selected map.
#include "gb_tile_example.h"
u8 example_tiles[1024];
u8 example_attrs[1024];
void __memset(void* dest, u8 value, u16 len);
void __settilebg16_buf(u8* buf, u8 x, u8 y, u8 tile);
void __settilebg16cgb_buf(u8* tilebuf, u8* attrbuf, u8 x, u8 y, u8 tile, u8 attr);
void __settilebg16_flush(const u8* buf, u8 y, u8 x, u8 count);
void __settilebg16cgb_flush(const u8* tilebuf, const u8* attrbuf, u8 y, u8 x, u8 count);

void main() {
    u8 failures;
    failures = 0;
    tile_example_begin();
    __memset(example_tiles, 0, 1024);
    __memset(example_attrs, 0, 1024);
    __settilebg16cgb_buf(example_tiles, example_attrs, 1, 1, 'A', 2);
    // The buffer operation must not write to VRAM yet.
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C42, 0) != 0) { failures++; }
    // Transfer the prepared cell so its four characters can be seen.
    __settilebg16cgb_flush(example_tiles, example_attrs, 1, 2, 2);
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C42, 0) != 'A') { failures++; }
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C43, 0) != 'B') { failures++; }
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C62, 0) != 'C') { failures++; }
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C63, 0) != 'D') { failures++; }
    if (example_tiles[66] != 'A') { failures++; }
    if (example_tiles[99] != 'D') { failures++; }
    if (tile_example_read(0x9C44, 0) != 0) { failures++; }
    if (example_attrs[66] != 2) { failures++; }
    if (example_attrs[99] != 2) { failures++; }
    if (__cgb_is_cgb() && tile_example_read(0x9C42, 1) != 2) { failures++; }
    if (__cgb_is_cgb() && tile_example_read(0x9C63, 1) != 2) { failures++; }
    tile_example_finish(failures, 1);
}

Expected result

The selected map shows the written characters or filled area. The program reads back the addressed tile bytes and, on CGB, the attribute bytes; FAILED CHECKS 000 means those comparisons passed. Both maps initially contain zero, and the example selects 0x9C00 for BG/window before the demonstrated call, so a fixed-map call can be distinguished from a selected-map call. These examples perform the writes with the LCD off; they do not measure LCD-on timing.

The visible cell contains AB above CD, at tile coordinates (2,2). This is one 16×16-pixel cell at cell coordinates (1,1). Buffer examples first verify that RAM preparation leaves VRAM unchanged, then flush the cell; flush examples prepare the RAM bytes explicitly before transferring them.

All four characters are blue on CGB because the four attribute bytes are 2. They are black on DMG.

__settilebg16cgb_flush

Transfer two adjacent tile rows from the RAM buffer to the LCDC-selected BG map. The source offset is 64*y + x; count bytes are copied from that row and from the row 32 bytes below it.

Write a tile number and its CGB attribute. On DMG, only the tile-number write is performed. On CGB, enter with VRAM bank 0 selected; attributes use bank 1 and the call finishes with VBK=0.

Waits for writable VRAM when necessary. The LCD-on path uses interrupt masking and can enable interrupts afterward; it is not a promise to preserve the caller's interrupt state or to finish within one VBlank.

Syntax

c
__settilebg16cgb_flush(tilebuf, attrbuf, y, x, count);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

tilebuf, attrbuf

Readable tile-map buffer with a 32-byte row stride. A full map occupies 1024 bytes. The two-buffer form takes separate tile-number and attribute arrays with the same layout; it does not interleave them.

y, x, count

Argument order is y,x,count. y is a 16-pixel cell row (0–15); x and count are 8-pixel tile units. Keep x+count <= 32. For one cell at (2,3), use y=3,x=4,count=2.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

The example uses gb_common.h: m_init() loads the supplied ASCII font with character codes as tile numbers. m_wait(); M_LCDC=0; stops the LCD during VBlank before unsafe transfers. The final LCDC value selects which map is visible.

__smac16

Compute a signed multiply-accumulate.

Syntax

c
u16 __smac16(u16 acc, u16 a, u8 b);

Parameters

acc

16-bit accumulator to add.

a

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

b

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

Return value

Each term is trunc(a*b/256), added to acc; returns the low 16 bits.

Conditions and limits

GB products are divided by 256; signed results truncate toward zero. Q1.7 variants double that truncated result and can differ by one from exact division by 128. Terms are rounded separately; final addition wraps at 16 bits.

Usage example

c
// Compare literal coefficients with values read from RAM.
result[26]=__smac16(65500,-513,-64);
v0=65500;v1=-513;v2=-64;
result[27]=__smac16(v0,v1,v2);
// Reverse coefficient signs and verify negative products.
result[28]=__smac16(65500,-513,64);
v0=65500;v1=-513;v2=64;
result[29]=__smac16(v0,v1,v2);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Compare literal inputs with values stored in RAM. Representative results appear as unsigned 16-bit values; negatives use two’s-complement bit patterns. GB rescales fixed-point products, while FC returns integer products, so identical inputs need not give identical results.

The excerpt stores these 16-bit values: result[26]=92, result[27]=92, result[28]=65372, result[29]=65372. Each literal-input calculation matches its RAM-input counterpart. The screen shows representative values; the result array holds every result.

Read one SRAM byte at a CPU address.

Syntax

c
u8 __sram_read8(u16 address);

Parameters

address

CPU address in $A000..$BFFF.

Return value

Returns the byte without checking RAM presence or data validity.

Conditions and limits

Writes 0x0A to $0000 to enable RAM before access, then writes zero to disable it afterward. Does not select the bank or validate the address; the caller configures the RAM bank. No save header or checksum is managed.

Usage example

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Save three bytes, 7/42/255, then test length mismatch, an invalid slot and a damaged checksum. A successful load yields middle byte 42; a failed read preserves destination 77; validation after clearing returns 0.

__svbk_get

Read the effective WRAM bank mapped at $D000–$DFFF. The compiler reads SVBK bits 0–2 and converts raw selector 0 to bank 1. This returns a bank number, not RAM capacity, an address or a pointer.

Syntax

c
u8 __svbk_get();

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Return value

Current effective bank number as u8, 1–7; raw selector 0 is reported as 1.

Conditions and limits

__svbk_get and __svbk_set require --cgb=cgb_only or #pragma rom_cgb cgb_only. DMG and dual-mode builds reject them with KQ2103, even if a runtime condition would skip the call. Use the guarded raw setter only when its different contract fits your program.

Switching banks changes every access in $D000–$DFFF; fixed WRAM at $C000–$CFFF stays mapped. Keep the stack and all state needed during the switch outside the switched window. The sample uses --stack-bank=fixed and explicitly located fixed-WRAM state. Coordinate interrupts and banked DMA with the switch; these APIs add no critical section.

Usage example

c
if (__svbk_get()!=1) failures++; // Normalize raw selector zero to effective bank 1.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The complete CGB-only program stores 1 at $D100 in WRAM bank 2 and 2 at the same address in bank 3, then reads both back and restores bank 1. The values choose an 8 × 8 red square at (16,24) and a blue one-pixel 8 × 8 square outline at (16,48). FAILED CHECKS 000 checks raw-selector normalization, bank separation and the previous-bank return for constant, variable, arithmetic and function-result arguments. Six separate invalid-build fixtures verify KQ2103 for DMG/dual targets and KQ2102 for constant banks 0 and 8. Runtime verification uses KOKURA; real hardware and interrupt-driven concurrent bank changes are not tested.

__svbk_set

Switch the WRAM bank mapped at $D000–$DFFF and return the effective bank selected before the switch. Save this return value if you need to restore the caller's bank. The memory contents are not copied or cleared, and the function does not restore the bank automatically.

Syntax

c
u8 __svbk_set(u8 bank);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

bank

Requested bank as u8, 1–7. Constant values outside this range produce KQ2102. Dynamic values are not range-checked by this intrinsic; validate them before calling rather than relying on register masking.

Return value

Effective bank number before the switch as u8, 1–7. This is the old bank, not the newly selected bank.

Conditions and limits

__svbk_get and __svbk_set require --cgb=cgb_only or #pragma rom_cgb cgb_only. DMG and dual-mode builds reject them with KQ2103, even if a runtime condition would skip the call. Use the guarded raw setter only when its different contract fits your program.

Switching banks changes every access in $D000–$DFFF; fixed WRAM at $C000–$CFFF stays mapped. Keep the stack and all state needed during the switch outside the switched window. The sample uses --stack-bank=fixed and explicitly located fixed-WRAM state. Coordinate interrupts and banked DMA with the switch; these APIs add no critical section.

previous_bank=__svbk_set(requested_bank);
if(previous_bank!=1 || __svbk_get()!=2) failures++;
*((u8*)0xD100)=1; // This byte belongs to bank 2.
previous_bank=__svbk_set(next_bank()); // Dynamic argument evaluates to 3.
if(previous_bank!=2 || __svbk_get()!=3) failures++;
*((u8*)0xD100)=2; // Same CPU address, different physical RAM.

__vram_memcpy_unsafe

Copy len bytes from src to dst immediately, in increasing address order. The function returns after the copy finishes; it does not enqueue work. Source and destination advance by one byte, without tilemap row strides or tile-format conversion.

Syntax

c
void __vram_memcpy_unsafe(u16 dst, const void* src, u16 len);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

Parameters

dst

First destination byte address, normally in VRAM 0x8000–0x9FFF. Keep the entire span valid. CGB uses the current VRAM bank; bank 0 contains tile numbers and bank 1 contains map attributes. These routines do not choose a map from LCDC, wrap rows or allocate VRAM.

src

Source byte pointer, valid and mapped for the whole call. Data is read immediately; it is not retained for a later flush. The source bank is not switched automatically. Use non-overlapping spans: this forward copy does not provide memmove semantics.

len

Number of consecutive bytes, 0–65535. It is not a tile count. Keep the complete address range inside valid source and writable destination storage; the API does not check bounds or prevent 16-bit address wrap.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Skip all LCD/STAT waiting and write directly with the CPU. Keep the LCD off, or ensure the entire transfer fits in a writable interval you control. Merely entering VBlank does not make an arbitrarily long transfer safe. This intrinsic emits neither DI nor EI for the transfer and provides no clipping or bounds checks.

Usage example

c
// The LCD is off throughout these unchecked writes.
__vram_memcpy_unsafe(0x98C2,strip,computed_length());

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This example uses __vram_memcpy_unsafe to place three map bytes at tile (2,6), pixel (16,48). Expect the three patterns [1,2,3] from left to right in a 24 × 8 area. Neighboring cells must remain blank. The full program places each tested copy or fill on its own row.

The supplied original graphics use tile 1 for a solid 8 × 8 square, tile 2 for its left four columns, and tile 3 for a left-aligned triangle that widens by one pixel per row from 1 to 8 pixels. DMG uses black on white; CGB distinguishes the operations with colors while keeping text black.

The square at pixel (16,88) must remain after zero-length safe and unsafe calls. With the LCD on, safe copy and fill add squares at (16,96) and (32,96). FAILED CHECKS must read 000. The emulator tests compare the drawn pixels as well as the counter. CGB uses bank 0 in this example; other banks and physical hardware are not tested here.

In CGB mode, the operation rows from MEMCPY through FILL UNSAFE cycle through red, blue and green. The ZERO COUNT square is red. In LCD ON, the left square is blue and the right square is green. Text stays black. The checks verify these colors at every drawn pixel.

__vram_memset_unsafe

Immediately fill len consecutive bytes starting at dst with the byte value. This repeats one byte, not a whole tile pattern. A map-byte fill repeats a tile number; a pattern-byte fill instead changes the encoded pixel planes.

Syntax

void __vram_memset_unsafe(u16 dst, u8 value, u16 len);

The parameter names in this call syntax explain the compiler intrinsic; they are not a separate C prototype.

dst

value

One byte, 0–255, written repeatedly. Its visible meaning depends on whether the destination contains tile indices, pixel planes or another byte-based structure.

len

Number of consecutive bytes, 0–65535. It is not a tile count. Keep the complete address range inside valid source and writable destination storage; the API does not check bounds or prevent 16-bit address wrap.

physics2d.h — 2D motion and collision

Provides box integration/AABB contacts and an optional surface-response solver. Bodies use centers and half extents; active=0 excludes a slot and inv_mass_q8<=0 makes it static. KQRect instead uses top-left coordinates and width/height. Box-pair contacts do not use the body restitution field; surface responses use KQSurface2D coefficients.

Choose consistent integer units for positions, radii, half extents, velocities and gravity. One step is one simulation tick. The samples use one unit per pixel. These routines neither convert positions to Q8.8 automatically nor render them.

A world borrows its array. The caller allocates and owns body storage and keeps it alive. Initializing a world does not initialize its array elements.

__smul16x8

Multiply a signed 16-bit value by a signed 8-bit coefficient, divide by 256 and truncate toward zero.

Syntax

c
s16 __smul16x8(s16 a, s8 b);

Parameters

a

Signed 16-bit value to scale.

b

Signed byte coefficient in -128..127.

Return value

Returns the signed 16-bit scaled product.

Conditions and limits

The coefficient range is -128..127, scaled with 256 representing 1.0. Products truncate toward zero for either sign: -257*64/256 returns -64.

Usage example

c
result[13]=__smul16x8(-257,64);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Left shows the initial state; right shows one tick later. A red 16x16 box with center (24,24) and velocity (4,16) reaches (28,36), with Y velocity zero on the blue floor. Panel origins are screen (8,48) and (88,48). DMG renders all marks in black. RAM checks also cover initialization, setters, integration, rectangle/point queries and signed scaling.

rpg.h — Random numbers, text, maps, saves and RPG/ADV/SLG services

Absolute text helpers draw directly on the background map. text_window opens a framed area, text_clear_rect fills a region, and text_print_xy writes tile bytes without control decoding. text_print_u8, text_print_u16 and text_print_s16 convert numbers to decimal with only the required cells. Reserve and clear a full field when replacing values of different lengths.

The RNG functions declared in rpg.h are implemented in lib/rng.c. They share the compiler's GB generator: rng_seed resets it, rng8/rng_next8 consume one byte, rng16/rng_next16 consume two, and rand_range/rng_range, rng_chance and weighted_choice adapt draws for gameplay choices. Compile rng.c with your program when calling these library functions. For reproducible tests, keep the seed and call order fixed; modulo-based choices do not promise exact probabilities.

RLE decoding uses count/value byte pairs and a zero count terminator. rle_decode reads an ordinary pointer into RAM; rle_decode_far reads a ROM-bank-qualified pointer into RAM; __rle_decode_vram expands banked input directly to VRAM with LCD-aware stores. The RAM functions live in lib/rle.c, while the direct VRAM operation is compiler-generated. All three return output bytes and require a valid stream and enough destination space.

Game-state storage declared in rpg.h is implemented by lib/flags.c. The three flag functions operate on 2048 independent Boolean bits; quest_state and quest_set_state operate on 64 independent bytes for game-defined stages. Compile flags.c when using them, keep IDs within those limits, and use a separate save system if progress must survive power-off.

Windowed dialogue shares one active rectangle, cursor and character-speed setting. text_open initializes the area, text_close erases it, and text_set_speed sets per-character VBlank waits. text_print and text_print_far interpret control streams; text_choice runs a blocking vertical selector. Load the tiles, fit the area and plan how the game handles these blocking calls.

Provides map/metatile drawing, scripts, SRAM saves and pathfinding. Ordinary cells are 8×8 pixels; metatiles are 16×16. Loading/drawing, movement masks and attack masks are separate operations; the game coordinates graphics loading and event execution.

Search uses about 4 KiB of shared, non-reentrant workspace. Limit maps to 1024 cells and explored distances to 254. Distance 0xFF means unreached, so a 255-step route is not representable. Cost/mask outputs need width*height writable bytes.

Defaults to four 512-byte slots, each with a six-byte header and up to 506 payload bytes. The sample uses MBC5 with 8 KiB SRAM. Calls finish with RAM disabled and do not restore its previous bank or enable state.

Menus support both blocking selection and separate input/draw calls driven by the game loop. The inventory menu displays item names and quantities.

__bit_clear

Clear the selected flag to 0 without clearing the rest of its byte. Use this to remove one stored condition, such as a temporary status flag. Clearing the same bit again still leaves it at 0.

Syntax

c
void __bit_clear(u8* p, u16 bit_index);

Parameters

p

Pointer to the first byte of the flag array in CPU-accessible memory. The array is not allocated or initialized by this call. Use writable RAM for set, clear and toggle operations; the test operation only reads it.

bit_index

Zero-based bit index as u16 (0–65535), not a byte offset or a bit mask. Index 0 selects mask 0x01 in byte 0; index 7 selects 0x80 in byte 0; index 8 selects 0x01 in byte 1. In general, the byte offset is index / 8 and the mask is 1 << (index % 8). For an N-byte array, require index < 8*N and a valid CPU address range.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

The caller must provide enough storage. There is no array-length argument, bounds clipping, bank switching or automatic graphics upload. A large bit number can select a byte well beyond the allocated array. Keep the memory mapping stable; do not use these RAM-flag helpers as a shortcut for hardware registers whose reads or writes have side effects.

Set, clear and toggle read a byte, modify the selected bit, then write the byte back. This sequence is not an atomic update. Coordinate writers in the main loop and interrupt handlers so that an intervening update to another bit in the same byte is not lost.

Usage example

c
__bit_clear(bit_flags,2);
bit_clear_value=bit_flags[0]; // A6 & FB = A2, decimal 162.
__bit_clear(bit_flags,2);     // Clearing it twice leaves it clear.

__bit_set

Set the selected flag to 1 while preserving the other seven bits in the same byte. For example, mark a quest as completed or an item as collected. Setting a bit that is already 1 leaves it unchanged; this is not a toggle.

Syntax

c
void __bit_set(u8* p, u16 bit_index);

Parameters

p

Pointer to the first byte of the flag array in CPU-accessible memory. The array is not allocated or initialized by this call. Use writable RAM for set, clear and toggle operations; the test operation only reads it.

bit_index

Zero-based bit index as u16 (0–65535), not a byte offset or a bit mask. Index 0 selects mask 0x01 in byte 0; index 7 selects 0x80 in byte 0; index 8 selects 0x01 in byte 1. In general, the byte offset is index / 8 and the mask is 1 << (index % 8). For an N-byte array, require index < 8*N and a valid CPU address range.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

The caller must provide enough storage. There is no array-length argument, bounds clipping, bank switching or automatic graphics upload. A large bit number can select a byte well beyond the allocated array. Keep the memory mapping stable; do not use these RAM-flag helpers as a shortcut for hardware registers whose reads or writes have side effects.

Set, clear and toggle read a byte, modify the selected bit, then write the byte back. This sequence is not an atomic update. Coordinate writers in the main loop and interrupt handlers so that an intervening update to another bit in the same byte is not lost.

Read one flag from a packed array of bits without modifying the array. This lets eight independent on/off flags share each byte of RAM. The result tells you whether the selected bit is clear or set; its numeric representation depends on the target.

Syntax

c
u8 __bit_test(const u8* p, u16 bit_index);

Parameters

p

Pointer to the first byte of the flag array in CPU-accessible memory. The array is not allocated or initialized by this call. Use writable RAM for set, clear and toggle operations; the test operation only reads it.

bit_index

Zero-based bit index as u16 (0–65535), not a byte offset or a bit mask. Index 0 selects mask 0x01 in byte 0; index 7 selects 0x80 in byte 0; index 8 selects 0x01 in byte 1. In general, the byte offset is index / 8 and the mask is 1 << (index % 8). For an N-byte array, require index < 8*N and a valid CPU address range.

Return value

u8: exactly 0 when the bit is clear, or 1 when it is set. The GB implementation normalizes the masked byte to these two values.

Conditions and limits

The caller must provide enough storage. There is no array-length argument, bounds clipping, bank switching or automatic graphics upload. A large bit number can select a byte well beyond the allocated array. if(bit_on!=0)bit_is_on=1; // The same nonzero test works on both targets.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

void EmitRamMemcpyLoop(string labelPrefix)
    {
        AsmOperand loop = MakeUniqueLabel(labelPrefix + "_loop");
        AsmOperand done = MakeUniqueLabel(labelPrefix + "_done");

        EmitLabel(loop);
        EmitAsm("LD_A_B");
        EmitAsm("OR_C");
        EmitAsm("JR_Z", done);
        EmitAsm("LD_A_DE");
        EmitAsm("LDI_HL_A");
        EmitAsm("INC_DE");
        EmitAsm("DEC_BC");
        EmitAsm("JR", loop);
        EmitLabel(done);
    }

__far_memcpy

Temporarily select a ROM bank, copy len bytes from src to dst in increasing address order, then restore the compiler’s saved ROM bank. __farmemcpy and __far_memcpy use the same implementation on this platform.

Syntax

c
void __far_memcpy(void* dst, u8 bank, const void* src, u16 len);

Parameters

dst

Destination in writable memory. Reserve enough space for every byte copied. Except for a zero-byte transfer, a null or invalid destination is not checked.

bank

8-bit bank selector for the source ROM mapping. Use a bank supported by the cartridge and the compiler’s bank layout; this argument is separate from the source address.

src

Near pointer to readable source bytes in the selected ROM bank. It does not contain a bank number.

len

Byte count, 0–65535. Zero performs no memory copy, but the bank-selection and restoration steps still run.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Keep the full source range in the intended ROM mapping and the full destination range in writable memory. Copying does not select the next bank at a window boundary, handle overlapping ranges like memmove, or provide VRAM-safe writes. Use the graphics transfer APIs for VRAM.

The samples place calling code in fixed bank 0 so source-bank changes cannot unmap the code being executed. These transfers are synchronous. Do not interrupt a transfer with another bank-changing copy or assume the helper makes a whole application interrupt-safe.

The GB helper restores the compiler’s ROM-bank shadow. Use __bankswitch to maintain it; raw writes to the mapper do not update that shadow. Its saved-bank slot in HRAM is shared, so nested transfers that overwrite it are unsafe.

Usage example

c
__far_memcpy(buffer,2,asset_shapes,32); // Same backend as __farmemcpy.
expect(*asset_bank_marker==0xA1,29);
for(i=0;i<32;i++) expect(buffer[(__safe_index u8)i]==expected_shape_byte(i),32);
buffer[32]=0x55;
__far_memcpy(buffer+32,2,asset_shapes,0); // Zero count writes no bytes and restores the bank.
expect(buffer[32]==0x55 && *asset_bank_marker==0xA1,30);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Copy two patterns, 32 bytes, from payload bank 2 while bank 1 is initially selected. The program compares every copied byte, checks that bank 1 is restored and verifies that a zero-length copy leaves a 0x55 sentinel unchanged.

Expected image: a red row starts at pixel (16,32) and spans 72×8 pixels. It repeats an 8×8 triangle, an 8×8 square outline with a one-pixel border, and a tile with its left four columns filled, three times. The triangle grows from one pixel at the top left to eight pixels on its bottom row.

On GB, a blue triangle and outline at (16,64) show the __farmemcpy result; a green pair at (16,96) shows __far_memcpy. Each pair occupies 16×8 pixels. CGB shows these colors; DMG shows the same shapes in black on white.

Expected status: FAILED CHECKS 000 and FIRST FAILURE 00. The verification runs 300 frames and compares text, shape masks and colors against these expectations. This is emulator evidence, not a physical-hardware test.

__fill_tilemap

__fill_tilemap is a compiler alias for __vram_memset. It uses the same byte-count argument and the same immediate CPU transfer, including its LCD-access rules.

Immediately fill len consecutive bytes starting at dst with the byte value. This repeats one byte, not a whole tile pattern. A map-byte fill repeats a tile number; a pattern-byte fill instead changes the encoded pixel planes.

Syntax

c
void __fill_tilemap(u16 dst, u8 value, u16 len);

Parameters

dst

First destination byte address, normally in VRAM 0x8000–0x9FFF. Keep the entire span valid. CGB uses the current VRAM bank; bank 0 contains tile numbers and bank 1 contains map attributes. These routines do not choose a map from LCDC, wrap rows or allocate VRAM.

value

One byte, 0–255, written repeatedly. Its visible meaning depends on whether the destination contains tile indices, pixel planes or another byte-based structure.

len

Number of consecutive bytes, 0–65535. It is not a tile count. Keep the complete address range inside valid source and writable destination storage; the API does not check bounds or prevent 16-bit address wrap.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Supply an explicit starting address and byte count. This alias neither chooses the background map nor fills a whole map automatically. For one complete 32 × 32 tile-number map, use its base address and 1024 bytes with VRAM bank 0 selected.

With the LCD on, each byte write waits for STAT mode 0 or 1 under DI and is followed by EI. With the LCD off, a plain CPU loop is used. The call can span frames, does not preserve an interrupt-disabled entry state, and does not program DMA registers. Zero length performs no data transfer.

Usage example

c
__fill_tilemap(0x9922,1,length_base+length_extra); // Explicit address and byte count, not a whole-map clear.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This example uses __fill_tilemap to fill three map bytes at tile (2,9), pixel (16,72), with tile number 1. Expect a solid 24 × 8 bar with blank neighboring cells. The count is computed from variables or a function result; all three bytes must still receive value 1.

The supplied original graphics use tile 1 for a solid 8 × 8 square, tile 2 for its left four columns, and tile 3 for a left-aligned triangle that widens by one pixel per row from 1 to 8 pixels. DMG uses black on white; CGB distinguishes the operations with colors while keeping text black.

The square at pixel (16,88) must remain after zero-length safe and unsafe calls. With the LCD on, safe copy and fill add squares at (16,96) and (32,96). FAILED CHECKS must read 000. The emulator tests compare the drawn pixels as well as the counter. CGB uses bank 0 in this example; other banks and physical hardware are not tested here.

In CGB mode, the operation rows from MEMCPY through FILL UNSAFE cycle through red, blue and green. The ZERO COUNT square is red. In LCD ON, the left square is blue and the right square is green. Text stays black. The checks verify these colors at every drawn pixel.

__memcpy

Copy a caller-specified number of bytes from src to dst. The 16-bit count supports transfers longer than 255 bytes, such as copying a complete RAM table. Bytes are read and written in ascending address order.

Syntax

c
void __memcpy(void* dst, const void* src, u16 count);

Parameters

dst

Pointer to the first writable destination byte. Reserve enough consecutive bytes for the complete operation; no buffer is allocated for you.

src

Pointer to the first readable source byte. The entire range must remain accessible and unchanged throughout the copy.

count

Number of bytes as u16 (0–65535), not an element count. The type's maximum is not a promise that such a large valid buffer exists on the target machine. Keep the whole range within the selected memory mapping.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

A zero count transfers no bytes. Side effects in argument expressions still occur: the example calls two pointer-returning functions and observes both calls even though the copy length is zero.

Use separate, non-overlapping source and destination ranges. These routines copy forward and do not provide overlap-safe memmove behavior; writing into the unread part of the source can corrupt later bytes.

The operation finishes before the caller continues. It neither switches ROM/RAM banks nor clips a range to a buffer boundary. Keep mappings stable, use valid memory ranges and coordinate access with interrupt handlers that use the same buffers.

On GB, these are ordinary CPU memory accesses. They do not wait for safe VRAM/OAM access, start DMA or select a CGB VRAM/WRAM bank. Use the dedicated graphics-transfer APIs for those jobs.

Usage example

c
memory_reset();
__memcpy(memory_destination+1,memory_source+1,257);
memory_copy_word=memory_check(257,0); // 257 copied bytes; guards unchanged.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This example uses __memcpy to copy 257 patterned bytes starting at offset 1. memory_check compares the entire source and destination arrays; the COPY WORD row must show 257. Starting inside the buffer leaves a leading guard byte, and bytes after the payload must also remain unchanged.

The complete program resets two 264-byte buffers before each operation, then checks every source byte, every destination byte and the untouched guard regions. The expected rows are COPY WORD 257, FILL WORD 257, COPY BYTE 255, FILL BYTE 255, COPY16 016, COPY32 032, ZERO CALLS 002 and FAILED 000. WORD/BYTE describe the count width, not the size of each copied item. The numbers are produced by the sample's checks, not return values from these void functions.

The captured screens show black lettering on white for DMG, blue on white for CGB and blue on black for FC. This example verifies RAM operations; the lettering presents the results rather than demonstrating a drawing primitive. Separate emulator checks cover 88 memory cases on each platform, including constant and runtime lengths at 0, 1, 16, 17, 32, 33, 64, 65 and 255 bytes, plus 256 and 257 for the word-count forms. Physical hardware has not been tested.

__memcpy_small

Copy a block of at most 255 bytes using an 8-bit count. Use this form when the transfer length fits in a byte. _small describes the count width; it is not a promise of a particular execution time or generated code size.

Syntax

c
void __memcpy_small(void* dst, const void* src, u8 len);

Parameters

dst

Pointer to the first writable destination byte. Reserve enough consecutive bytes for the complete operation; no buffer is allocated for you.

src

Pointer to the first readable source byte. The entire range must remain accessible and unchanged throughout the copy.

len

Number of bytes as u8: 0–255. Do not pass 256 to mean a full 256-byte block; that length does not fit this parameter. Use the corresponding function without _small for 256 bytes or more.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

A zero count transfers no bytes. Side effects in argument expressions still occur: the example calls two pointer-returning functions and observes both calls even though the copy length is zero.

Use separate, non-overlapping source and destination ranges. These routines copy forward and do not provide overlap-safe memmove behavior; writing into the unread part of the source can corrupt later bytes.

The operation finishes before the caller continues. It neither switches ROM/RAM banks nor clips a range to a buffer boundary. Keep mappings stable, use valid memory ranges and coordinate access with interrupt handlers that use the same buffers.

On GB, these are ordinary CPU memory accesses. They do not wait for safe VRAM/OAM access, start DMA or select a CGB VRAM/WRAM bank. Use the dedicated graphics-transfer APIs for those jobs.

Usage example

c
memory_reset();
__memcpy_small(memory_destination+1,memory_source+1,255);
memory_copy_byte=memory_check(255,0); // Maximum representable byte count.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This example uses __memcpy_small to copy 255 patterned bytes starting at offset 1. memory_check compares the entire source and destination arrays; the COPY BYTE row must show 255. Starting inside the buffer leaves a leading guard byte, and bytes after the payload must also remain unchanged.

The complete program resets two 264-byte buffers before each operation, then checks every source byte, every destination byte and the untouched guard regions. The expected rows are COPY WORD 257, FILL WORD 257, COPY BYTE 255, FILL BYTE 255, COPY16 016, COPY32 032, ZERO CALLS 002 and FAILED 000. WORD/BYTE describe the count width, not the size of each copied item. The numbers are produced by the sample's checks, not return values from these void functions.

The captured screens show black lettering on white for DMG, blue on white for CGB and blue on black for FC. This example verifies RAM operations; the lettering presents the results rather than demonstrating a drawing primitive. Separate emulator checks cover 88 memory cases on each platform, including constant and runtime lengths at 0, 1, 16, 17, 32, 33, 64, 65 and 255 bytes, plus 256 and 257 for the word-count forms. Physical hardware has not been tested.

__memset

Write the same byte value throughout a destination range. The 16-bit count is useful for clearing a large buffer or initializing a table. For example, filling with 0x5A writes 5A 5A 5A…; it does not repeat a multibyte integer.

Syntax

c
void __memset(void* dst, u8 value, u16 count);

Parameters

dst

Pointer to the first writable destination byte. Reserve enough consecutive bytes for the complete operation; no buffer is allocated for you.

value

The byte repeated at every destination address: 0–255. Use 0 to clear the range. To initialize a u16 array to a nonzero numeric value, assign its elements individually instead.

count

Number of bytes as u16 (0–65535), not an element count. The type's maximum is not a promise that such a large valid buffer exists on the target machine. Keep the whole range within the selected memory mapping.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

A zero count transfers no bytes. Side effects in argument expressions still occur: the example calls two pointer-returning functions and observes both calls even though the copy length is zero.

The operation finishes before the caller continues. It neither switches ROM/RAM banks nor clips a range to a buffer boundary. Keep mappings stable, use valid memory ranges and coordinate access with interrupt handlers that use the same buffers.

On GB, these are ordinary CPU memory accesses. They do not wait for safe VRAM/OAM access, start DMA or select a CGB VRAM/WRAM bank. Use the dedicated graphics-transfer APIs for those jobs.

Usage example

c
memory_reset();
__memset(memory_destination+1,0x5A,257);
memory_fill_word=memory_check(257,1); // Repeat one byte, not a 16-bit word.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.
